\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p03-vaught-two-cardinal}{cited=Vaught1965CardinalsFarApart}{Vaught's two-cardinal theorem}
Let \(T\) be a countable first-order theory in a language containing a unary
predicate \(U\). If \(T\) has a model \(M\) with
\(|M|>|U^M|\ge\aleph_0\), then \(T\) has a model \(N\) with
\(|N|=\aleph_1\) and \(|U^N|=\aleph_0\). The countability of the language and
the distinguished unary predicate are part of the statement; the theorem does
not prescribe arbitrary pairs of infinite cardinals.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p03-nonforking-calculus}{cited=TentZiegler2012}{Nonforking in stable theories}
Let \(T\) be stable.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item If \(A\subseteq B\) and \(p\) is a complete finite-tuple type over
        \(A\), then \(p\) has an extension to \(B\) that does not fork over
        \(A\).
  \item For tuples \(a,b\), the type \(\operatorname{tp}(a/Ab)\) does not
        fork over \(A\) iff \(\operatorname{tp}(b/Aa)\) does not fork over
        \(A\).
  \item If \(A\subseteq B\subseteq C\) and \(p\) is a complete type over
        \(C\), then \(p\) does not fork over \(A\) iff both \(p\) does not
        fork over \(B\) and \(p\mathbin{\upharpoonright}B\) does not fork
        over \(A\).
\end{enumerate}
Thus nonforking has extension, symmetry, and transitivity.  Moreover,
\(\omega\)-stable theories are superstable and superstable theories are
stable; neither converse holds.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p03-ominimal-cell-decomposition}{cited=VanDenDries1998}{O-minimal cell decomposition}
For every finite family of definable subsets of \(M^n\), there is a finite
partition of \(M^n\) into cells such that each set in the family is a union of
cells.  If finitely many definable functions are also specified, the partition
can be refined so that each restriction to every cell contained in its domain
is continuous.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p03-nip}{Shattering, IP, and NIP}
Let \(T\) be complete and let \(\varphi(x;y)\) be a formula.  In a model
\(\mathcal M\entails T\), the parameter family
\(\{\varphi(\mathcal M;b):b\in(\dom\mathcal M)^{\abs y}\}\)
\emph{shatters} a finite set
\(A\subseteq(\dom\mathcal M)^{\abs x}\) when, for every \(A_0\subseteq A\),
some parameter tuple \(b\) satisfies
\(\varphi(\mathcal M;b)\cap A=A_0\).  The formula has the
\emph{independence property (IP) in \(T\)} when arbitrarily large finite sets are
shattered in some model of \(T\); it is \emph{NIP} otherwise.  The theory
\(T\) is NIP when every formula is NIP.  Formula-level shattering and
theory-level NIP are distinct standings; the latter is used in the dividing
line comparison below.
\index{independence property}
\index{NIP}
\index{shattering}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p03-fol-zero-one}{cited=Fagin1976}{FO zero--one law}
For every first-order \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\), if \(\mathcal A_n\) is
uniformly random among the labeled \(\tau\)-structures with universe \([n]\),
then
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\mathcal A_n\entails\varphi]
  \quad\text{exists and belongs to }\{0,1\}.
\]
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{annexitem}{annex:p3.abstract.3}{thm:p03-lindstrom}{Lindstr\"om's theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix an \(\mathcal L^*\)-sentence \(\alpha\) and reduce to its finite
relational occurrence signature \(\tau\).  Any constants in \(\tau\) may be
replaced definitionally by fresh unary predicates required to be singletons;
we therefore write the coding below for relation symbols only.

\emph{The finite sequence code.}
Use unary predicates \(U,V,Q_U,Q_V\), constants \(e_U,e_V\), ternary
relations \(A_U(s,a,s')\), \(A_V(t,b,t')\), and a four-place relation
\(H(s,t,a,b)\).  The intended structures have \(U,V\) as disjoint
\(\tau\)-domains, \(Q_U,Q_V\) as their finite-sequence sorts, \(e_U,e_V\) as
empty sequences, and \(A_U,A_V\) as one-coordinate append.  The graph coded
by a pair \((s,t)\) is
\[
 h_{s,t}=\{(a,b):H(s,t,a,b)\}.
\]
The following is a single first-order formula because \(\tau\) is finite:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Piso}(s,t)\;\defeq{}&
  \forall a\,b\bigl(H(s,t,a,b)\to U(a)\land V(b)\bigr)\\
 &\land\forall a\,b\,b'
   \bigl(H(s,t,a,b)\land H(s,t,a,b')\to b=b'\bigr)\\
 &\land\forall a\,a'\,b
   \bigl(H(s,t,a,b)\land H(s,t,a',b)\to a=a'\bigr)\\
 &\land\bigwedge_{R\in\tau}\forall\bar a\,\bar b
   \left(\bigwedge_{j<\operatorname{arity}(R)}H(s,t,a_j,b_j)
     \to\bigl(R(\bar a)\leftrightarrow R(\bar b)\bigr)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(\operatorname{Seq}\) be the finite conjunction saying that the four
unary sorts are pairwise disjoint, \(U,V\) are nonempty,
\(Q_U(e_U)\), \(Q_V(e_V)\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\forall a\,b\,\neg H(e_U,e_V,a,b),\\
 &\forall s\,a\bigl(Q_U(s)\land U(a)\to
      \exists s'\,(Q_U(s')\land A_U(s,a,s'))\bigr),\\
 &\forall t\,b\bigl(Q_V(t)\land V(b)\to
      \exists t'\,(Q_V(t')\land A_V(t,b,t'))\bigr),\\
 &\forall s\,a\,s'\bigl(A_U(s,a,s')\to
      Q_U(s)\land U(a)\land Q_U(s')\bigr),\\
 &\forall t\,b\,t'\bigl(A_V(t,b,t')\to
      Q_V(t)\land V(b)\land Q_V(t')\bigr),\\
 &\forall s\,t\,a\,b\,s'\,t'\bigl(
 A_U(s,a,s')\land A_V(t,b,t')\ \to{}\\[-2mm]
 &\qquad\forall x\,y\left(
 H(s',t',x,y)\leftrightarrow
   \bigl(H(s,t,x,y)\lor(x=a\land y=b)\bigr)\right)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The constants \(e_U,e_V\) are temporary constants allowed by the regular
logic's fresh-constant clause.  Only append chains starting at
\((e_U,e_V)\) will be used, so the displayed equations determine every graph
used in the argument after a standard finite number of steps.

\emph{Potential isomorphism preserves \(\mathcal L^*\)-truth.}
Add a binary relation \(I(s,t)\) and let \(\operatorname{BF}(I)\) be the
first-order conjunction
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &I(e_U,e_V),\qquad
   \forall s\,t\bigl(I(s,t)\to
      Q_U(s)\land Q_V(t)\land\operatorname{Piso}(s,t)\bigr),\\
 &\forall s\,t\,a\bigl(I(s,t)\land U(a)\to
   \exists b\,s'\,t'\,[V(b)\land A_U(s,a,s')\land A_V(t,b,t')
       \land I(s',t')]\bigr),\\
 &\forall s\,t\,b\bigl(I(s,t)\land V(b)\to
   \exists a\,s'\,t'\,[U(a)\land A_U(s,a,s')\land A_V(t,b,t')
       \land I(s',t')]\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
If potentially isomorphic structures \(A,B\) disagreed on \(\alpha\), first
replace a witnessing back-and-forth family by its downward closure.  It remains
a back-and-forth family, and whenever a member is extended to cover one new
element, restricting the larger map to the old graph plus that one pair gives
an exact one-pair extension still in the family.  Interpret \(I(s,t)\) on the
actual paired finite sequences exactly when their coordinate map belongs to
this downward-closed family.  The actual append operations then interpret
\(\operatorname{Seq}\land\operatorname{BF}(I)\).
Unary relativization to \(U,V\) turns the disagreement into
\(\alpha^U\land\neg\alpha^V\).  Thus the one
\(\mathcal L^*\)-sentence
\[
 \operatorname{Seq}\land\operatorname{BF}(I)
 \land\alpha^U\land\neg\alpha^V
\]
would be satisfiable.  Downward L\"owenheim--Skolem gives a countable model.
Enumerate its \(U\)- and \(V\)-sorts, start with \((e_U,e_V)\), and use the
two extension clauses alternately.  After \(n\) steps, the update axiom makes
\(h_{s_n,t_n}\) a finite map with at most \(n\) pairs, and
\(\operatorname{Piso}\) makes it a partial isomorphism.  The maps increase,
their union is total and onto, and it is therefore an isomorphism of the two
reducts.  Isomorphism invariance contradicts their disagreement on
\(\alpha\).  Hence potentially isomorphic structures agree on every
\(\mathcal L^*\)-sentence.

\emph{Bounded rank gives a first-order definition.}
Write \(A\equiv_mB\) when \(A,B\) agree on first-order sentences of
quantifier rank at most \(m\).  For fixed finite \(\tau\) and \(m\), there
are only finitely many such theories.  Prove simultaneously in \(m,n<\omega\)
that, up to logical equivalence, there are only finitely many formulas of
quantifier rank at most \(m\) whose free variables lie among the fixed list
\(x_1,\ldots,x_n\).  At \(m=0\), the finite relational signature and fixed
variable list give finitely many atoms, hence finitely many Boolean truth
functions of those atoms.  At the successor stage, every formula is equivalent
to a Boolean combination of atoms and formulas
\(\exists x_{n+1}\,\psi(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1})\), where \(\psi\) has rank at
most \(m\); the induction hypothesis at \((m,n+1)\) again leaves only
finitely many possibilities.  Taking \(n=0\) proves the sentence claim.
Choose one finite characteristic conjunction for each
\(\equiv_m\)-class.  If \(\equiv_m\) always makes structures agree on
\(\alpha\), the disjunction of exactly the characteristic conjunctions whose
classes satisfy \(\alpha\) is a first-order sentence equivalent to
\(\alpha\).

\emph{Compactness produces potential isomorphism.}
Suppose no such \(m\) exists.  Choose \(A_m,B_m\) with
\[
 A_m\equiv_mB_m,\qquad A_m\entails\alpha,\qquad B_m\not\entails\alpha.
\]
Duplicator therefore wins the \(m\)-round EF game on \(A_m,B_m\).

Extend the finite sequence vocabulary by a unary number sort \(N\), temporary
constants \(0,c\) permitted by the fresh-constant clause, a strict order
\(<\), a binary successor relation \(S\), and a ternary relation
\(W(r,s,t)\).  Let \(\operatorname{Disc}(N,0,S,<)\) be the finite
first-order conjunction saying that \(<\) is a strict linear order on \(N\),
\(0\) is its least element, every element has a unique immediate successor,
and every nonzero element has a unique immediate predecessor, with
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &N(0)\land\forall r\,(N(r)\to\neg(r<0)),\\
 &\forall r\,(N(r)\to\exists!r'\,S(r,r')),\\
 &\forall r\,(N(r)\land r\ne0\to\exists!r'\,S(r',r)),\\
 &\forall r\,r'\left(S(r,r')\leftrightarrow
   \bigl(N(r)\land N(r')\land r<r'
     \land\neg\exists q\,(N(q)\land r<q\land q<r')\bigr)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(\Theta\) be the conjunction of \(\operatorname{Disc}\),
\(\operatorname{Seq}\), \(N(c)\),
\(\alpha^U\land\neg\alpha^V\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &W(c,e_U,e_V),\\
 &\forall r\,s\,t\bigl(W(r,s,t)\to
      N(r)\land Q_U(s)\land Q_V(t)\land\operatorname{Piso}(s,t)\bigr),\\
 &\forall r\,r'\,s\,t\bigl(S(r,r')\land W(r',s,t)\to{}\\
 &\quad [\forall a\,(U(a)\to\exists b\,s'\,t'\,
      (V(b)\land A_U(s,a,s')\land A_V(t,b,t')\land W(r,s',t')))]\\
 &\quad\land[\forall b\,(V(b)\to\exists a\,s'\,t'\,
      (U(a)\land A_U(s,a,s')\land A_V(t,b,t')\land W(r,s',t')))]\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
All conjuncts except the two relativized occurrences of \(\alpha\) are
first-order, so \(\Theta\) is one \(\mathcal L^*\)-sentence in the declared
finite signature of relation symbols and temporary constants.  Compactness
and downward L\"owenheim--Skolem apply uniformly to such fresh-constant
expansions by the regular logic's abstraction clause.

For each standard \(k\), use the first-order sentence
\[
 \beta_k(c)\ \defeq\
 \exists x_0\cdots x_k\left(
   x_0=0\land\bigwedge_{i<k}S(x_i,x_{i+1})\land x_k<c\right),
 \qquad
 \Gamma=\{\Theta\}\cup\{\beta_k(c):k<\omega\}.
\]
Thus no successor term has been added to the relational signature.  Every
finite subset is satisfiable: choose \(m\) larger than all its displayed chain
lengths,
interpret \(c\) by \(m\), use \(A_m,B_m\) as the \(U,V\)-reducts, and let
\(W(r,s,t)\) record the positions from which Duplicator can survive \(r\)
more rounds.  Countable compactness gives a model of \(\Gamma\), so \(c\) is
above every standard numeral.

Externally define \(r_0=c\), and let \(r_{k+1}\) be the unique predecessor of
\(r_k\).  Each \(r_k\) exists and is nonzero because the model satisfies
\(\beta_k(c)\) for every standard \(k\).  Let
\(\mathcal I_k\) contain exactly the graphs \(h_{s,t}\) for which
\(W(r_k,s,t)\) holds and there are paired append chains of length \(k\) from
\((e_U,e_V)\) to \((s,t)\).  Then \(\mathcal I_0\) contains the empty map.
The update axiom makes every member of \(\mathcal I_k\) a finite map with at
most \(k\) pairs, and the \(W\)-axiom makes it a partial isomorphism.  If
\(h_{s,t}\in\mathcal I_k\) and \(a\in U\), the forth clause produces paired
appends \(s',t'\) with \(W(r_{k+1},s',t')\); the update equation says that
\(h_{s',t'}\) extends \(h_{s,t}\) and contains \(a\) in its domain.  The back
clause gives the symmetric range extension.  Hence
\(\bigcup_{k<\omega}\mathcal I_k\) is a back-and-forth family of finite
partial isomorphisms: the two reducts are potentially isomorphic.

But \(\Theta\) says that those reducts disagree on \(\alpha\), contradicting
the potential-isomorphism result already proved.  Therefore a finite \(m\)
exists, the bounded-rank argument gives a first-order sentence equivalent to
\(\alpha\), and the arbitrary \(\mathcal L^*\)-sentence \(\alpha\) was
first-order definable.  The reverse expressive inclusion is part of the
definition of regular abstract logic.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{proofboundary}{def:p04-church-turing}{Church--Turing thesis}
The \emph{Church--Turing thesis} identifies the informally understood
effectively calculable numerical functions with the Turing-computable
functions.  Church proposed identifying effective calculability with
lambda-definability---equivalently, by Kleene's theorem, general
recursiveness---while Turing analyzed machine computation.  The equivalence
and robustness of the resulting formal models support the identification
\cite{Church1936,Kleene1936,Turing1937Lambda,
Soare1996ComputabilityRecursion}.  They do
not prove it, because ``effective calculability'' is the informal explicandum,
not an independently formalized class quantified over by a theorem.  The
thesis stated here is not the claim that every physical process is Turing
computable, and formal-model equivalence does not imply equality of complexity
costs (the named formalism-versus-complexity warning in
Section~\ref{sec:turing-machines-01}).
\index{Church--Turing thesis}
\end{proofboundary}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p04-degree-operations}{Join and jump on degrees}
For \(A,B\subseteq\N\), put
\[
 A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}.
\]
Define the join of \(\deg_T(A)\) and \(\deg_T(B)\) to be
\(\deg_T(A\oplus B)\).  Lemma~\ref{thm:p04-degree-semilattice} verifies that
this operation is independent of representatives and is their least upper
bound.  The monotonicity in
Remark~\ref{rem:jump-convention} makes
\[
 \deg_T(A)'\defeq\deg_T(A')
\]
well defined.  Write \(\mathbf0=\deg_T(\varnothing)\) and
\(\mathbf0'=\deg_T(\varnothing')\).  A \emph{c.e. degree} is the degree of
some computably enumerable set.  These are derived operations and subclasses
of the already defined degree order, not additional primitive relations.
\index{Turing degree!join}
\index{Turing degree!jump}
\index{computably enumerable degree}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p4.degrees.2}{thm:p04-kleene-post}{Kleene--Post incomparability theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the fixed oracle-program numbering \((\varphi_e^B)_{e<\omega}\).  Build
increasing strings \(\sigma_s,\tau_s\in2^{<\omega}\); their unions are the
characteristic functions of \(A\) and \(B\).  Meet, alternately,
\[
 R_e:\chi_A\not\simeq\varphi_e^B,
 \qquad S_e:\chi_B\not\simeq\varphi_e^A.
\]
Every candidate Turing reduction occurs in this list.  Given an oracle decider,
compile it to a numerical oracle program that writes \(1\) and accepts after
the simulated accept, and writes \(0\) and accepts after the simulated reject.
Its computed function is the target characteristic function.  The wrapper is
a primitive-recursive finite-table transformation, and the fixed serialization
of row tags, states, symbols, targets, and query rows produces its valid code.
For a finite oracle string \(\tau\), the notation
\(\varphi_e^\tau(x)\mathord\downarrow=i\) means that the finite computation
halts with value \(i\) and every oracle query is below \(\operatorname{len}(\tau)\),
answered by \(\tau\).

At the \(R_e\)-stage choose
\(x\geq\operatorname{len}(\sigma_s)\), pad \(\sigma_s\) with zeros below
\(x\), and ask \(\varnothing'\) whether
\[
 \exists\tau'\supseteq\tau_s\;
       \varphi_e^{\tau'}(x)\mathord\downarrow=0.
\]
This is a c.e. question about finite strings and finite computations.  By the
cited completeness theorem for \(K\),
Theorem~\ref{thm:arithmetical-hierarchy-classification}, it reduces many-one
to \(K\).  Given an
ordinary index \(p\), a primitive-recursive table compiler produces a
query-free oracle program that ignores its input and simulates
\(\varphi_p(p)\); its code belongs to \(\varnothing'\) exactly when
\(p\in K\).  Hence the question is decidable by \(\varnothing'\), without
using the sketched convention bridge.  If the
answer is yes, effectively find the least witnessing \(\tau'\), adopt it, and
set \(\sigma_{s+1}(x)=1\).  If the answer is no, retain \(\tau_s\) and set
\(\sigma_{s+1}(x)=0\).  Pad both new strings so their lengths exceed \(x\).
The \(S_e\)-stage interchanges \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\).  Also pad at every
stage beyond the stage number, so both unions are total.

Each requirement, once treated, is permanent.  In the yes case the chosen
finite oracle computation remains convergent with value \(0\) under every
later oracle extension, while the target bit is \(1\).  In the no case no
later extension can make that value \(0\); the final computation therefore
diverges or has a value different from the target bit \(0\).  Hence all
\(R_e,S_e\) hold, so \(A\not\leq_TB\) and \(B\not\leq_TA\).

The entire stage construction is computable in \(\varnothing'\).  To decide
the \(n\)-th bit of either limit, run it until the corresponding string has
length greater than \(n\); thus \(A,B\leq_T\varnothing'\).  Neither is
computable, since a computable set reduces to every oracle.  Neither has
degree \(\mathbf0'\), because if, for example,
\(\varnothing'\leq_TA\), then \(B\leq_T\varnothing'\leq_TA\), contrary to
incomparability.  Their degrees are therefore incomparable and strictly
between \(\mathbf0\) and \(\mathbf0'\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p4.degrees.4}{thm:p04-friedberg-muchnik}{Friedberg--Muchnik theorem}
\begin{proof}
List
\[
 R_e:\varphi_e^B\not\simeq\chi_A,
 \qquad S_e:\varphi_e^A\not\simeq\chi_B
\]
in the priority order \(R_0>S_0>R_1>S_1>\cdots\).  Use the fixed effective
oracle-program numbering.  Write
\(\varphi^{B_s}_{e,s}(x)\mathord\downarrow=y\) when the first \(s\) steps of
program \(e\), with each oracle query answered by membership in the finite set
\(B_s\), halt accepting with valid output \(y\).  Its use is one plus the
largest queried number, or \(0\) if no query occurs.  A finite computation is
determined by the oracle below its use: if all later approximations agree with
\(B_s\) there, it is the final \(B\)-oracle computation; conversely every
halting final computation appears at a sufficiently late stage once its finite
oracle segment stabilizes.  These claims follow by induction through the
finitely many transition steps.

Every candidate Turing reduction appears among the requirements.  Wrap its
oracle decider so that a simulated accept writes \(1\) and accepts, while a
simulated reject writes \(0\) and accepts; the resulting total numerical
function is the target characteristic function.  Normalizing and serializing
that finite table is primitive recursive and does not rely on the sketched
relativized-adequacy theorem.

At stage \(s\), a finite state records
\(A_s,B_s\), and, for each of the first \(s\) strategies, either no witness or
one witness, a satisfaction flag, and a restraint bound; bound \(0\) encodes
the empty restraint.  Visit the first \(s\) strategies in priority order.
This is a fair computable scheduler because every strategy is visited at every
sufficiently large stage.

An initialized \(R_e\) chooses a fresh witness \(x>s\), larger than every
active higher-priority restraint and every reserved witness, and keeps
\(x\notin A_s\).  Search the finite stage computation for
\(\varphi_{e,s}^{B_s}(x)\mathord\downarrow=0\).  When it appears, let \(u\)
be one plus the largest oracle query, or \(0\) if there was no query; enumerate
\(x\) into \(A\), impose the \(B\)-restraint \(u\), mark \(R_e\) satisfied,
and initialize every lower-priority strategy.  Initialization cancels its
witness, flag, and restraint but never removes an enumerated number.  A lower
strategy chooses all later witnesses above the active higher restraints, so
it cannot change the protected oracle segment.  The \(S_e\)-strategy is the
same construction with \(A,B\) interchanged.  Each stage performs finitely
many bounded simulations and finite-state updates, so the two stage unions are
c.e.; the fixed scheduler and universal numbering give their enumeration
indices effectively.

We verify requirements by induction through the priority order.  Assume all
higher strategies have stabilized.  They act only finitely often, so the
current strategy is initialized only finitely often and eventually chooses a
final witness.  Suppose for contradiction that
\(\varphi_e^B=\chi_A\).  If \(R_e\) acts on its final witness, the preserved
computation has value \(0\) while that witness enters \(A\), a contradiction.
If it never acts, the final witness stays outside \(A\), so total equality
would give a convergent value \(0\).  That computation has finite use.  Since
witnesses are chosen above their stages, only finitely many later lower-priority
enumerations can occur below that use; after the oracle segment stabilizes,
the stage simulation sees the value \(0\) and \(R_e\) acts, again a
contradiction.  Thus \(R_e\) is met; the proof for \(S_e\) is symmetric.

Every oracle program occurs in the fixed enumeration, so the requirements
give \(A\not\leq_TB\) and \(B\not\leq_TA\).  Neither set is computable.  Every
c.e. set is Turing reducible to \(\varnothing'\): from an enumeration index
and a number \(n\), compile a query-free oracle program that writes \(0\) and
accepts exactly when that enumeration lists \(n\), and ask
\(\varnothing'\) whether its code is in
the jump.  If either constructed set had
degree \(\mathbf0'\), the other would reduce to it, contradicting
incomparability.  Hence both c.e. degrees lie strictly between
\(\mathbf0\) and \(\mathbf0'\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-myhill}{cited=Myhill1955}{Myhill isomorphism theorem}
If \(A\leq_1B\) and \(B\leq_1A\), then some computable permutation
\(\pi:\N\to\N\) satisfies
\[
 x\in A\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\pi(x)\in B.
\]
Consequently, any two creative sets are computably isomorphic.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-rice-shapiro}{cited=Johnson1977Rice}{Rice--Shapiro theorem}
For \(d\in\N\), let \(D_d\) be the finite subset of \(\N\) whose members are
the positions of the \(1\)-bits in the binary expansion of \(d\).  Let
\(\mathcal C\) be a class of c.e. subsets of \(\N\), and let
\(I_{\mathcal C}=\{e:W_e\in\mathcal C\}\) be its extensional index set.
Then \(I_{\mathcal C}\) is computably enumerable if and only if there is a
computably enumerable set \(\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathcal C}\subseteq\N\) of
finite-set codes such
that, for every c.e. set \(W\),
\[
 W\in\mathcal C
 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
 \exists d\in\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathcal C}\;(D_d\subseteq W).
\]
The empty class is included by allowing
\(\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathcal C}=\varnothing\).
Thus a positive c.e. extensional property is witnessed by finite positive
information.  The result concerns extensional index sets of c.e. sets, not
arbitrary semantic properties of programs; within that scope it is stronger
than Rice's undecidability classification.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-kolmogorov-invariance}{cited=LiVitanyi2008}{Invariance theorem}
There is an optimal plain machine \(U_C\) such that, for every partial
computable decompressor \(V\), some constant \(c_V\) satisfies
\[
 C_{U_C}(x)\leq C_V(x)+c_V
 \qquad\text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^*.
\]
There is likewise a universal optimal prefix-free machine \(U_K\).  More
precisely, for every prefix-free partial computable machine \(V\), there is a
finite binary string \(\sigma_V\) such that
\[
 U_K(\sigma_Vp)\simeq V(p)\qquad\text{for every }p\in\{0,1\}^*,
\]
where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.  The strings \(\sigma_V\) are
chosen from a prefix-free effective coding of machines, so that
\(\operatorname{dom}(U_K)\) remains prefix-free.  Consequently
some constant \(d_V\) satisfies
\[
 K_{U_K}(x)\leq K_V(x)+d_V
 \qquad\text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^*.
\]
Each constant depends on the two machines but not on \(x\).  Thus complexity
is invariant only up to an additive machine-dependent constant
\cite{Kolmogorov1965}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-chaitin-incompleteness}{cited=Chaitin1974}{Chaitin-style incompleteness}
Fix the optimal prefix-free machine \(U_K\), an arithmetic coding of strings and
programs.  Let \(\mathsf{Run}_{U_K}(p,x,t)\) be the bounded arithmetic
formula asserting that \(t\) codes a valid halting computation of \(U_K\) on
\(p\) with output \(x\).  This bounded arithmetic formula is needed because
\(U_K\) uses the separately fixed prefix-machine and string coding.  It is an
object-language computation predicate, not a machine relation; unlike the
inherited \(\mathsf{Comp}(e,x,s)\), its machine index is fixed and its input
is a binary program string.  A primitive-recursive compiler between the two
finite trace codings preserves acceptance, and
\(\mathsf{Run}_{U_K}\) is used only in the following theory hypothesis and
complexity sentence.

Let \(T\) be a computably axiomatized arithmetic
theory with a primitive-recursive proof relation such that every true closed
instance of \(\mathsf{Run}_{U_K}\) is provable in \(T\), and interpret
\(K_{U_K}(x)>n\) by the \(\Pi^0_1\) sentence saying that no program of length
at most \(n\) has such a computation.  Assume \(T\) is \(\Pi^0_1\)-sound:
every \(\Pi^0_1\) sentence it proves is true in \(\N\).

Then there is a constant \(b_{T,U_K}\) such that \(T\) proves no sentence
\(K_{U_K}(x)>n\) with \(n>b_{T,U_K}\).  The bound depends on \(T\), \(U_K\),
the proof relation, and the coding; mere consistency is not substituted for
the displayed soundness and computation-representation hypotheses.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-time-hierarchy}{cited=HartmanisStearns1965}{Deterministic time hierarchy theorem}
If \(f\) and \(g\) are time-constructible and
\(f(n)\log f(n)=o(g(n))\), then
\[
 \mathsf{DTIME}(f(n))\subsetneq\mathsf{DTIME}(g(n)).
\]
In particular, \(\mathsf P\subsetneq\mathsf{EXPTIME}\).  The
constructibility and simulation-overhead gap are hypotheses of the theorem,
not optional regularity assumptions \cite[thm.~3.1]{AroraBarak2009}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-space-hierarchy}{cited=StearnsHartmanisLewis1965}{Deterministic space hierarchy theorem}
If \(f\) and \(g\) are space-constructible and \(f(n)=o(g(n))\), then
\[
 \mathsf{SPACE}(f(n))\subsetneq\mathsf{SPACE}(g(n)).
\]
In particular,
\(\mathsf{PSPACE}\subsetneq\mathsf{EXPSPACE}\)
\cite[thm.~3.2]{AroraBarak2009}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p04-tqbf-pspace}{proved=annex:p9.tqbf.1}{TQBF completeness}
The language \(\mathsf{TQBF}\) is \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\)-complete under
polynomial-time many-one reductions.  Both membership and hardness are part
of the statement.  The historical source role is
\textcite{StockmeyerMeyer1973}; a complete handbook proof is
Annex~\ref{annex:p9.tqbf.1} \cite[thm.~4.11]{AroraBarak2009}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p05-tennenbaum}{cited=Tennenbaum1959}{Tennenbaum's theorem}
No countable nonstandard \(\mathcal M\entails\PA\) has a computable
presentation.  Explicitly, there is no bijection
\(e:\N\to\dom\mathcal M\) for which both transported operations
\[
  (m,n)\longmapsto e^{-1}\!\bigl(e(m)+^{\mathcal M}e(n)\bigr),\qquad
  (m,n)\longmapsto e^{-1}\!\bigl(e(m)\times^{\mathcal M}e(n)\bigr)
\]
are computable functions on \(\N^2\).  This does not deny the existence
of countable nonstandard models, and it does not claim that their order
has no computable copy \cite{Kaye1991}.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p05-countable-pa-order-type}{cited=Kaye1991}{Order type of a countable nonstandard model of PA}
Let \(\mathcal M\entails\PA\) be countable and nonstandard.  Under the
arithmetic order, its standard initial segment has order type \(\omega\),
each finite-distance block has order type
\(\operatorname{otp}(\mathbb Z,<)\), and the quotient order of the nonstandard
blocks is a countable dense linear order without endpoints.  Consequently
\[
  \operatorname{otp}(\dom\mathcal M,<^{\mathcal M})
  =\omega+\sum_{q\in(\mathbb Q,<)}\operatorname{otp}(\mathbb Z,<).
\]
The sum is the lexicographic sum indexed by \((\mathbb Q,<)\), with one copy of
\((\mathbb Z,<)\) at every index; it fixes the meaning of the
convention-sensitive shorthand \(\omega+\mathbb Z\cdot\mathbb Q\).  For an
uncountable nonstandard model the
block quotient remains dense without endpoints but need not have order
type \(\mathbb Q\).
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p05-interpretation-transfer}{cited=TMR1953}{Interpretation transfer}
If \(\mathcal I\) interprets \(U\) in \(V\), then
\[
  U\derives\psi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  V\derives\psi^{\mathcal I}.
\]
Consequently, consistency of \(V\) implies consistency of \(U\).  If,
in addition, \(U\) is essentially undecidable, \(V\) is consistent and
computably enumerable, and the interpretation is effective, then \(V\)
is essentially undecidable and hence undecidable.  Plain undecidability
alone does not generally transfer under an arbitrary interpretation.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p05-sigma-one-completeness}{proved=annex:p5.sigma.1}{External and formalized Sigma-one completeness}
Let \(\sigma\) be a closed \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence in its original syntax.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item If \(\mathcal N\entails\sigma\), then
        \(\mathsf Q\derives\sigma\).  Hence every theory extending
        \(\mathsf Q\) proves every true closed \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence.
  \item For the literal selected PA proof predicate
        \(\mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}(p,x)\defeq
          \Gamma_{d_{19}}(p,x,\bar1)\) and its existential closure
        \(\mathsf{Prv}^{19}_{\PA}(x)\) from
        Definition~\ref{def:p05-selected-direct-pa-graph}, the following is a
        metatheoretic schema over closed \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentences:
        \[
          \PA\derives
          \sigma\to
          \mathsf{Prv}^{19}_{\PA}(\overline{\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner}).
        \]
\end{enumerate}
The first clause is external truth-to-provability; the second internalizes
for each fixed sentence the specified proof construction of
\cref{thm:p05-original-sigma-evidence,annex:p5.original-sigma-evidence},
from bounded evidence that includes dependent existential witnesses.
The resulting proof record ends at the code of \(\sigma\) in its
original syntax. Neither clause is a reflection
principle, and neither licenses
\(\mathsf{Prv}^{19}_{\PA}(\overline{\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner})\to\sigma\)
\cite{Shoenfield1967,HilbertBernays1939}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p5.sigma.1}{thm:p05-sigma-one-completeness}{External and formalized Sigma-one completeness}
Fix a closed \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence \(\sigma\) in its original syntax,
using the closure-style definition in
Table~\ref{tab:p04-arithmetical-hierarchy}. An existential witness below a
bounded universal may depend on the bounded variable. We first prove
bounded-instance completeness and then encode all finitely many dependent
witnesses in one evidence number. The fixed marked negation-normal-form
conversion determines its evidence; the concluding proof has the original
sentence as its root.

For a term \(t(\vec x)\) and a tuple \(\vec n\), let
\(\operatorname{val}_t(\vec n)\) be its value in \(\mathcal N\).
Structural recursion on \(t\) constructs a \(\mathsf Q\)-proof of
\[
 t(\overline{\vec n})=
 \overline{\operatorname{val}_t(\vec n)}.                            \tag{2}
\]
For variables and \(0\) this is immediate.  The successor case uses equality
congruence.  The addition and multiplication cases append, respectively, the
axioms \(x+0=x\), \(x+Sy=S(x+y)\), \(x\times0=0\), and
\(x\times Sy=(x\times y)+x\) once for each digit of the evaluated second
argument.  Thus the map from \(\vec n\) to the code of (2) is primitive
recursive, not merely computable by an unbounded proof search.

We now prove, simultaneously for every bounded formula
\(\theta(\vec x)\), the two numeral-instance clauses
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 \mathcal N\entails\theta(\vec n)
   &\Longrightarrow
   \mathsf Q\derives\theta(\overline{\vec n}),\\[2pt]
 \mathcal N\not\entails\theta(\vec n)
   &\Longrightarrow
   \mathsf Q\derives\neg\theta(\overline{\vec n}).
\end{array}                                                           \tag{3}
\]
The induction also constructs the proof codes primitive recursively from
\(\vec n\).

For an atomic equality, evaluate its two terms by (2).  Equal numeral values
give the equality by transitivity; unequal values give its negation by repeated
successor injectivity and \(Sx\ne0\). Bottom is refuted by the fixed
logical derivation of \(\neg\bot\). For comparisons retain the two actual
abbreviations
\[
 u\leq v\defeq\exists z\,(z+u=v),\qquad
 u<v\defeq\exists z\,(u+Sz=v).
\]
True numeral comparisons use their standard difference witness and (2).
False weak comparisons follow from \cref{lem:q-bounded-cases} and
the refutations of the resulting numeral equalities.

Here is the strict enumeration needed both for false numeral comparisons
and strict bounded quantifiers. Metainduction on \(m\) constructs a
\(\mathsf Q\)-proof that \(y<\bar m\) implies the disjunction of
\(y=\bar j\) for \(j<m\), with empty disjunction \(\bot\).
At zero, \(y+Sz=0\) contradicts \(y+Sz=S(y+z)\) and \(Sx\ne0\).
At \(m+1\), \(y+Sz=S\bar m\) gives \(y+z=\bar m\).
Split \(z\) using the zero-or-successor axiom. If \(z=0\), then
\(y=\bar m\). If \(z=Sw\), then \(y+Sw=\bar m\), and the
previous strict enumeration gives one of \(y=\bar j\) for \(j<m\).
These are exactly all cases below \(m+1\). Each step uses a fixed finite
proof template, so this construction is primitive recursive in \(m\).
For a false strict numeral comparison, substitute its first numeral in
this enumeration and refute every resulting equality. Finally the Boolean
cases append the corresponding fixed propositional derivations to the
recursively constructed proofs.

For a bounded existential
\(\exists y\leq t(\vec x)\,\eta(y,\vec x)\), evaluate the bound to \(m\).
If the formula is true, bounded search returns the least \(j\leq m\) for which
\(\eta(j,\vec n)\) is true; the positive induction clause, the numeral proof
of \(\bar j\leq\bar m\), and existential introduction give the required
proof.  If it is false, the negative induction clause supplies proofs of
\(\neg\eta(\bar j,\overline{\vec n})\) for every \(j\leq m\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:q-bounded-cases} replaces an arbitrary
\(y\leq\bar m\) by the finite disjunction
\(y=\bar0\lor\cdots\lor y=\bar m\); reasoning by cases proves the negation
of the bounded existential.  The bounded universal case is dual: use all
positive instance proofs and the same finite case split when it is true, and
use the least counterexample when it is false. For a strict bound use the
cases \(j<m\); when \(m=0\), the strict guard is contradictory, so its
universal is proved and its existential refuted without a matrix instance.
A weak zero bound has the single case \(j=0\). Each inner bound is
evaluated after its outer parameters and witnesses have been substituted.
All loops have the resulting finite bounds, so this completes both the
structural induction and the primitive-recursive construction in (3).

For the internal bounded-instance assertion, take the actual descriptions
\(d_\theta^+,d_\theta^-\) of
\cref{def:p05-fixed-bounded-builders}. These pack the specified raw trees
\(R_\theta^+,R_\theta^-\), with their respective success guards and zero
failure values. List the free indices of \(\theta\) as
\(i_1<\cdots<i_k\). Let \(s_\theta^+\) be the finite composition that
starts with \(\ulcorner\theta\urcorner\) and, in that order, applies
the selected \(\mathsf{sub}\) description at index \(i_j\) with the
numeral description \(\nu(x_j)\). Put
\(s_\theta^-=\mathsf{Neg}\circ s_\theta^+\), using the fixed
\(N_7\) constructor. These are exactly the descriptions denoted by
\(\theta^\nu(\vec x)\) and
\(\mathsf{Neg}(\theta^\nu(\vec x))\) in the bounded-builder theorem.
For \(k=0\), the first description is the constant original code.
The graph theorem \cref{thm:p05-pa-pr-graphs} gives existence and uniqueness
for each of these separately fixed descriptions, inside \(\PA\).

Theorem~\ref{thm:p05-fixed-bounded-builders}, proved in
\cref{annex:p5.fixed-bounded-builders}, therefore gives the following
formulas, with universal closure in \(\vec x\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \PA&\derives\theta(\vec x)\to\exists p\exists q\,\\
 &\quad(\Gamma_{d_\theta^+}(\vec x,p)\land
   \Gamma_{s_\theta^+}(\vec x,q)\land
   \mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}(p,q)),\\
 \PA&\derives\neg\theta(\vec x)\to\exists p\exists q\,\\
 &\quad(\Gamma_{d_\theta^-}(\vec x,p)\land
   \Gamma_{s_\theta^-}(\vec x,q)\land
   \mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}(p,q)).
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]
Here \(\mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}(p,q)\) is literally
\(\Gamma_{d_{19}}(p,q,\bar1)\). For example, uniqueness of the two
positive graph outputs turns the first line into the corresponding
implication for any supplied \(p,q\) satisfying those graphs. The cited
proof establishes the Boolean truth test, the safe-tree invariant, the
literal root after substitution, and all sentence and open-axiom factors
of that checker after packing. Its bounded folds retain dependent
parameters and both strict and weak zero-bound cases. Thus (4) uses the
internal equations and verification of these particular descriptions.

We now pass from bounded formulas to the full closure-style
\(\Sigma^0_1\) class. For every fixed \(\Sigma^0_1\)-formula
\(\varphi(\vec x)\), take precisely the fixed marked normal form
\(\rho=\mathcal N^+\varphi\) in
\cref{def:p05-signed-evidence-builders}. Define
\(E_\varphi(\vec x,e)\) to be an alias for the existing
\(\mathsf{Ev}_\varphi(\vec x,e)\) of
\cref{thm:p05-pa-sigma-evidence}: it is
\(\mathcal E_\rho(\vec x,e)\), with the very same fresh evidence
variable, auxiliary bound variables, conjunction associations and original
comparison binders as in
\cref{def:p05-positive-evidence-formation}. This is an assignment of a
fixed bounded formula, not an additional object-language predicate family.
For clarity, its clauses on the positive formation \(\rho\) are as
follows; the bounded-leaf clause always has priority.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item If the current \(\rho\) is bounded, use
        \(E_\rho(\vec x,e)\defeq(e=0\land\rho(\vec x))\).
        In particular a bounded original \(\varphi\) has the leaf
        \(e=0\land\mathcal N^+\varphi\).
  \item For \(\rho=\psi\land\chi\), use
        \[
        \exists u\leq e\,\exists v\leq e\,
          (\mathsf P(u,v,e)\land E_\psi(\vec x,u)
                             \land E_\chi(\vec x,v)).
        \]
        For \(\psi\lor\chi\), use
        \[
        \exists d<\bar2\,\exists v\leq e\,
          [\mathsf P(d,v,e)\land
            ((d=0\land E_\psi(\vec x,v))\lor
             (d=\bar1\land E_\chi(\vec x,v)))].
        \]
  \item For \(\rho=\exists y\,\psi(y,\vec x)\), use
        \[
        \exists y\leq e\,\exists v\leq e\,
          (\mathsf P(y,v,e)\land E_\psi(y,\vec x,v)).
        \]
        For a marked existential replace \(y\leq e\) by its original
        guard \(y\mathrel\diamond t(\vec x)\), where
        \(\diamond\in\{<,\leq\}\); retain \(v\leq e\).
  \item For
        \(\rho=\forall y\mathrel\diamond t(\vec x)\,\psi(y,\vec x)\), use
        \[
        E_\rho(\vec x,e)\defeq
        \forall y\mathrel\diamond t(\vec x)\,
        \exists v\leq e\,
          (\mathsf B(e,y,v)\land E_\psi(y,\vec x,v)),              \tag{5}
        \]
        where \(\mathsf B\) is the original bounded beta-entry formula of
        Lemma~\ref{lem:goedel-beta}.
\end{enumerate}
The weak guards \(u\leq e,v\leq e\) are the actual guards in
\(\mathsf{Ev}\); they are not replaced by \(u<Se,v<Se\).
Pairing components and beta entries are at most their respective code,
including at code zero. Every newly written quantifier is marked bounded.
Consequently each \(E_\varphi\) is bounded. The evidence number at a
bounded universal stores a possibly different existential-evidence object
for each bounded index; it is used in (5) and the two implications below.

Two metainductions on the fixed positive formation \(\rho\), followed
by its fixed logical equivalence to \(\varphi\), give
\[
 \mathsf Q\derives
   E_\varphi(\vec x,e)\to\varphi(\vec x),                          \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
 \PA\derives
   \varphi(\vec x)\to\exists e\,E_\varphi(\vec x,e).                \tag{7}
\]
Both displays have universal closure in their free numerical variables.
For (6), a bounded leaf follows by conjunction elimination. A conjunction
supplies evidence for both children; a disjunction supplies one of its two
tagged alternatives. Apply the child implications and the corresponding
propositional introductions. An existential supplies a witness and its
matrix evidence; apply the child implication and introduce that same
witness, retaining its original guard in a marked case. In the universal
case, (5) supplies matrix evidence for each \(y\) in its original range;
the child implication, guard discharge and universal introduction give
that marked universal. These steps use only first-order logic and so are
available in \(\mathsf Q\). They yield \(E_\varphi\to\rho\).
Each fixed negation-normal-form rewrite, including implication elimination,
double negation, De Morgan laws and quantifier duality, is a classical
first-order equivalence. Expanding a marked quantifier gives its bounded
duality while retaining its bound and comparison binder; no rewrite moves
a formula across a binder. Consequently \(\mathsf Q\derives
\rho\leftrightarrow\varphi\), and composition proves (6) for the
original syntax. Auxiliary variables are fresh, and an otherwise unused
assumption can be used by conjunction and projection before discharge.

The nonlogical existence step at a bounded universal in (7) is finite
evidence collection. For every formula \(R(i,u,\vec a)\), full induction
in \(\PA\) proves the scheme
\[
 \forall i<n\,\exists u\,R(i,u,\vec a)
 \ \to\
 \exists w\,\forall i<n\,\exists u\leq w\,
   (\mathsf B(w,i,u)\land R(i,u,\vec a)).                         \tag{8}
\]
This is \cref{lem:p05-pa-finite-collection}. Its proof inducts on \(n\)
with all parameters retained. At zero take \(w=0\). At \(Sn\), use
the induction hypothesis and choose the new witness at \(n\); the
internally proved extension lemma \cref{lem:p05-pa-beta-extension}
appends it while preserving the first \(n\) entries. The internal
pairing and beta lemma \cref{lem:p05-pa-pair-beta} bounds every entry by
the new code. These two cases prove (8) inside \(\PA\). Substitution
of \(Sm\) for \(n\) gives its weak-bound variant, including the
single witness at a weak zero bound.

For (7), a bounded leaf uses evidence zero. Pair the two child evidence
values at a conjunction, or the appropriate tag and child evidence at a
disjunction. At an existential pair its witness with the evidence of its
matrix; pairing bounds supply the weak evidence guards, and a marked
witness retains its original comparison. At a bounded universal use (8)
after the child existence implication, with
\(R(y,v,\vec x)=E_\psi(y,\vec x,v)\). Choose
\(n=t(\vec x)\) for a strict bound and \(n=St(\vec x)\) for a
weak bound. A strict zero bound uses the empty code and needs no matrix
witness. Inner witnesses and bounds keep all their outer parameters, so
this collection covers dependent witnesses. These are precisely the
evidence-existence derivations of
\cref{thm:p05-pa-sigma-evidence,thm:p05-evidence-projections} and
\cref{annex:p5.evidence-projections}. Composing with
\(\varphi\leftrightarrow\rho\) gives (7).

For the internal proof record, take the specified signed description
\(\widehat d_\varphi^+\) of
\cref{def:p05-signed-evidence-builders}. Its inputs are the original
free-parameter tuple in increasing index order, followed by evidence;
fixed tuple projections supply each child and the evidence Boolean test.
Theorems~\ref{thm:p05-original-sigma-evidence} and
\ref{thm:p05-pa-pr-graphs}, with the record verification in
\cref{annex:p5.original-sigma-evidence}, give, with universal closure,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \PA&\derives E_\varphi(\vec x,e)\to\exists p\exists q\,\\
 &\quad(\Gamma_{\widehat d_\varphi^+}(\vec x,e,p)\land
   \Gamma_{s_\varphi^+}(\vec x,q)\land
   \mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}(p,q)).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]
Here \(s_\varphi^+\) is the same finite numeral-substitution description
defined before (4), now for the fixed original \(\varphi\). To spell
out the bridge to (9), the signed theorem's premise
\(\mathcal E_\varphi^+\) is literally
\(\mathcal E_{\mathcal N^+\varphi}=E_\varphi\). Its safe-tree
conclusion has the original root \(\varphi^\nu\). The bounded-original
clause uses the two builders in (4) and the internally proved signed
Boolean identities (S1)--(S3) in
\cref{annex:p5.original-sigma-evidence}. The other signed clauses build
the original connective or quantifier: in particular, implication evidence
selects a proof of the negative antecedent or positive consequent, and the
output introduces the original implication. Marked collection uses the
actual arbitrary-matrix constructor of
\cref{thm:p05-bounded-case-elimination}, with the original guard and
the complete list of child proofs. Its empty strict and one-entry weak
zero cases are included.

The original numeral-instance root is a sentence. Packing the safe tree
therefore satisfies every factor of the selected \(d_{19}\) checker;
the outer successful evidence guard returns exactly that packed record.
Introduce the unique \(\Gamma_{\widehat d_\varphi^+}\) and
\(\Gamma_{s_\varphi^+}\) outputs to obtain (9). This is the
record-level consequence proved at the end of
\cref{annex:p5.original-sigma-evidence}; the normal form determines the
evidence, while the signed root calculation supplies the original code.

For the closed \(\sigma\), its parameter tuple is empty, so
\(s_\sigma^+\) is the constant \(\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner\) and
\(\widehat d_\sigma^+\) is unary. Eliminating the constant graph
output in (9) gives exactly
\[
 \PA\derives\forall e\,\bigl(E_\sigma(e)\to
  \exists p\,(\Gamma_{\widehat d_\sigma^+}(e,p)\land
   \mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}(p,\overline{\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner}))\bigr).
\]
Assume \(\sigma\) inside \(\PA\). By (7) choose its evidence
\(e\); the displayed implication gives a proof value \(p\).
Conjunction elimination gives its selected proof assertion. Existential
introduction in \(p\), elimination of the evidence witness, and discharge
of \(\sigma\) give
\[
 \PA\derives
 \sigma\to\exists p\,\mathsf{Prf}^{19}_{\PA}
   (p,\overline{\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner}),
\]
which is the formalized clause
\(\PA\derives\sigma\to
\mathsf{Prv}^{19}_{\PA}(\overline{\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner})\)
by \cref{def:p05-selected-direct-pa-graph}.

Finally suppose externally that \(\mathcal N\entails\sigma\). The fixed
logical equivalence gives \(\mathcal N\entails\mathcal N^+\sigma\).
Structural recursion on this positive formation chooses an ordinary finite
evidence number \(e\): use zero at a bounded leaf, pair at conjunction,
tag a true disjunct, and pair each existential witness with its matrix
evidence, retaining a marked witness's bound. At a bounded universal,
there are only finitely many indices and Lemma~\ref{lem:goedel-beta}
codes their separately chosen evidence objects. At a strict zero bound
there are none; a weak zero bound requires the single object at zero.
Thus \(\mathcal N\entails E_\sigma(\bar e)\).  The positive half of (3) gives
\(\mathsf Q\derives E_\sigma(\bar e)\), and (6) gives
\(\mathsf Q\derives\sigma\).  This proves the external clause and completes
both claims in the body theorem without a prefix-normal-form assumption.
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p05-solovay-completeness}{cited=Solovay1976}{Solovay arithmetical completeness}
For the selected \(\mathsf{Prv}^{19}_{\PA}\) and exactly the realizations of
Definition~\ref{def:p05-arithmetical-realization},
\[
 \mathsf{GL}\vdash A
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \PA\vdash A^*
 \text{ for every arithmetical realization }{^*}.
\]
The ambient metatheory uses the standard model
\(\mathcal N\entails\PA\), and hence the required external consistency and
\(\Sigma^0_1\)-soundness of this specific theory.  The display is not a theorem
about an arbitrary consistent or recursively axiomatized \(T\); changing the
base theory, numbering, or proof predicate requires a separately stated
generalization.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p05-gl-frames}{cited=Segerberg1971}{Finite-frame completeness of \(\mathsf{GL}\)}
\(\mathsf{GL}\) is sound and complete for the finite irreflexive transitive
Kripke frames under Definition~\ref{def:p05-gl-kripke}.  Equivalently, these
are finite strict partial orders in the displayed accessibility direction.
Finiteness already rules out infinite \(R\)-chains; in the unrestricted frame
formulation the corresponding additional condition is converse
well-foundedness.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p05-big-five}{The five standard subsystems}
Over \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\), define:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \(\mathsf{WKL}_0\) adds weak K\"onig's lemma: for every coded tree
        \(T\subseteq2^{<\N}\), if
        \(\forall n\,\exists s\in T\,(|s|=n)\), then there is
        \(P\subseteq\N\) such that \(P\upharpoonright n\in T\) for every
        \(n\);
  \item \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\) is the theory fixed in
        Definition~\ref{def:p05-full-aca}; equivalently, over
        \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\) it adds comprehension for every arithmetical
        formula, with number and set parameters;
  \item \(\mathsf{ATR}_0\) adds arithmetical transfinite recursion: if
        \((D,\prec)\) is a coded countable well-order and \(\theta\) is
        arithmetical, there is \(Y\subseteq D\times\N\) whose sections satisfy
        \[
          Y_i=\{n:\theta(i,n,Y^{<i},\bar A)\},
          \qquad
          Y^{<i}=\{\langle j,n\rangle:j\prec i
                         \text{ and }n\in Y_j\};
        \]
  \item \(\Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}_0\) adds the same comprehension axiom
        for every \(\Pi^1_1\) formula, allowing universal set quantifiers over
        an arithmetical matrix.
\end{itemize}
The collective label “Big Five” is needed only as a retrieval name for this
specific list, including the base \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\); it stands for five
distinct theories, not a sixth theory.  The added principles are
nonredundant, each theory is a subsystem of \(\mathsf Z_2\), and the list is
used in the calibration table and inclusion figure \cite{Simpson2009}.
\index{WKL0@\(\mathsf{WKL}_0\)}\index{ACA0@\(\mathsf{ACA}_0\)}
\index{ATR0@\(\mathsf{ATR}_0\)}\index{Pi11CA0@\(\Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}_0\)}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-cantor-normal-form}{cited=Jech2003}{Cantor normal form}
Every nonzero ordinal \(\alpha\) has a unique expression
\[
 \alpha=
 \omega^{\beta_0}\cdot n_0+
 \omega^{\beta_1}\cdot n_1+\cdots+
 \omega^{\beta_{k-1}}\cdot n_{k-1},
\]
where \(k\geq1\) is finite,
\(\beta_0>\beta_1>\cdots>\beta_{k-1}\), and each
\(n_i\in\N\setminus\{0\}\).  The coefficient is written on the right because
ordinal multiplication is not commutative.  The empty sum represents zero.
This is the \emph{Cantor normal form} of \(\alpha\)
\cite{Cantor1897,Sierpinski1965}.
\index{Cantor normal form}
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-konig-cardinal}{cited=Konig1905}{K\"onig's theorem}
Assume the Axiom of Choice.  Let \(I\) be a set and let
\(\langle\kappa_i:i\in I\rangle\) and
\(\langle\lambda_i:i\in I\rangle\) be families of cardinals such that
\(\kappa_i<\lambda_i\) for every \(i\in I\).  Then
\[
  \sum_{i\in I}\kappa_i
  <
  \prod_{i\in I}\lambda_i.
\]
In particular, for every infinite cardinal \(\kappa\),
\[
  \operatorname{cf}(2^\kappa)>\kappa
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \kappa^{\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)}>\kappa.
\]
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-hausdorff-recursion}{cited=Hausdorff1904}{Hausdorff's successor recursion}
Assume the Axiom of Choice.  For every infinite cardinal \(\kappa\) and every
nonzero cardinal \(\lambda\),
\[
  (\kappa^+)^\lambda
  =\kappa^\lambda\cdot\kappa^+
  =\max(\kappa^\lambda,\kappa^+).
\]
Equivalently, for ordinals \(\alpha,\beta\),
\[
  \aleph_{\alpha+1}^{\aleph_\beta}
  =\aleph_\alpha^{\aleph_\beta}\cdot\aleph_{\alpha+1}.
\]
The restriction \(\lambda\neq0\) cannot be dropped: the left side would be
\(1\) while the displayed product would be \(\kappa^+\).  Repeated use of
this identity is the Hausdorff recursion for exponentiation with a successor
aleph base \cite{Jech2003}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-easton}{cited=Easton1970}{Easton's theorem on regular cardinals}
Let \(F\) be a definable class function from the infinite regular cardinals to
cardinals such that
\(\kappa<\lambda\) implies \(F(\kappa)\leq F(\lambda)\), and
\(\operatorname{cf}(F(\kappa))>\kappa\) for every regular \(\kappa\).
Starting from a ground model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}+\mathsf{GCH}\) carrying such an
\(F\), Easton's forcing yields a cofinality-preserving generic extension in
which \(2^\kappa=F(\kappa)\) at every infinite regular cardinal \(\kappa\).
Thus monotonicity and K\"onig's cofinality condition are, relative to the
existence of the stated ground model, the only restrictions on the continuum
function at regular cardinals.  The theorem does not prescribe exponentiation
at singular cardinals and is a relative-consistency result, not a theorem that
\(\mathsf{ZFC}\) chooses one such function in the ground universe.
\end{hbtheorem}
